goals: Retell the story of Tricki’s illness and cure in your own words
Explain how pampering harms Tricki and how the vet cures him

slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study A Triumph of Surgery, a humorous story by the vet and writer James Herriot about a pampered little dog. Please read the story in your textbook, Footprints without Feet, before you go on. This lesson does not repeat the text. In the board exam, this reader is tested through short answers and long answers, so that is where we will focus.

slides.heading: How to use this lesson
bullets: Read the story once in *Footprints without Feet*.
Use these slides for the sequence of events, the themes and the characters.
The board asks 3-mark and 6-mark questions on this reader, not extracts: practise those most.
Explain events **in your own words**; do not memorise lines.
slides.narration: Here is how to use this lesson. Read the story first in your textbook. Then use these slides for the order of events, the themes and the characters. Remember that the board does not print extracts from this reader. It asks three mark and six mark questions on character, theme and values, so practise writing those answers in your own words.

visual.alt: Table of facts: the author is James Herriot, pen name of James Alfred Wight, 1916 to 1995, a British vet; the story comes from his humorous memoirs of country practice in Yorkshire; it is told in the first person by the vet; the main characters are Mrs Pumphrey, her Pekinese Tricki and the narrator.

slides.narration: James Herriot was the pen name of James Alfred Wight, a British vet who lived from nineteen sixteen to nineteen ninety-five. He wrote warm, funny memoirs about life as a country vet in Yorkshire. This story is told in the first person by the vet himself, so we see Mrs Pumphrey and her dog through the eyes of a sensible, amused professional.

slides.heading: The story in six stages
slides.body_md: From a shocking sight in the street to an ironic thank-you. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

visual.alt: Flow of the story in six stages: a shock in the street; advice ignored; Tricki falls ill; off to the surgery; recovery among other dogs; and the ironic triumph of surgery.
visual.caption: The story in six stages (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The story moves through six stages. The vet is shocked by Tricki in the street. His advice is ignored. Tricki falls seriously ill. The vet takes him to the surgery. There, Tricki recovers among other dogs. And finally his owner thanks the vet for what she calls a triumph of surgery. Keep this map in mind as we go through each stage.

slides.heading: Summary 1: a shock in the street
slides.body_md: The vet meets Mrs Pumphrey walking her Pekinese, Tricki, and is alarmed: the dog is badly overweight, sluggish and clearly unwell. Mrs Pumphrey thinks he is merely tired and underfed, so she has been giving him malt, cod-liver oil and Horlicks on top of cakes and sweets. The vet advises less food and more exercise.
slides.narration: The story opens in the street. The vet meets Mrs Pumphrey and her Pekinese, Tricki, and is alarmed to see how fat and unwell the dog has become. Mrs Pumphrey believes he is underfed, so she has been adding tonics such as malt and cod-liver oil to a diet full of sweets. The vet gently advises less food and more exercise.

slides.heading: Summary 2: advice ignored, Tricki falls ill
slides.body_md: Mrs Pumphrey cannot keep to the plan. Whenever Tricki seems unhappy or begs, she gives in. His condition worsens until he becomes seriously ill and the vet is called to the house.
slides.narration: The advice fails. Mrs Pumphrey loves Tricki too much to refuse him, so whenever he begs or looks sad, the treats return. His health goes from bad to worse, and at last he becomes seriously ill. Notice the cause and effect here. The owner’s indulgence, not any disease, is what has brought the dog to this state.

slides.heading: Check: the order of events
slides.narration: Your turn. Six events from the story are shuffled. Put them in order, from the meeting in the street to the moment Mrs Pumphrey collects her dog.

slides.heading: Summary 3: off to the surgery
slides.body_md: The vet decides that Tricki must stay at his surgery, where his diet and exercise can be controlled. Mrs Pumphrey is heartbroken, but she sends the dog off with his bed, his toys and his coats.
slides.narration: The vet now takes a firm decision. Tricki must leave home and stay at the surgery, where the vet can control what he eats and how much he moves. Mrs Pumphrey is heartbroken. Even so, she cannot let her darling go without his comforts, and the vet drives away with the dog, his bed, his toys and his coats.

slides.heading: Summary 4: recovery and the gifts
slides.body_md: At the surgery Tricki gets only water at first. Slowly he becomes interested in the other dogs, then runs and plays with them and eats eagerly at mealtimes. Meanwhile Mrs Pumphrey phones often and sends eggs and wine to strengthen him, which the vet and his colleagues enjoy themselves.
slides.narration: At the surgery, Tricki is given only water at first. Gradually his interest returns. He follows the other dogs, then runs and plays with them, and soon he is eating eagerly at mealtimes. Meanwhile Mrs Pumphrey phones often and sends eggs and wine to help him. The vet admits, with a smile, that he and his colleagues enjoyed those gifts themselves.

slides.heading: Summary 5: a triumph of surgery?
slides.body_md: When Tricki is fit again, Mrs Pumphrey comes to collect him. The slim, lively dog dashes to her, and she, overcome with joy, praises the vet and calls the cure a triumph of surgery. There was no operation at all.
slides.narration: Finally, Tricki is fit again, and Mrs Pumphrey comes to fetch him. The slim, lively dog rushes to her joyfully. Overcome with gratitude, she praises the vet and calls the recovery a triumph of surgery. But there was no operation. Plain food, exercise and company did the job. That gap between her belief and the truth is the irony of the title.

slides.heading: Theme 1: pampering versus real care
slides.body_md: Both characters love Tricki; only one helps him.
columns:
**Mrs Pumphrey’s care**

- sweets, cakes and tonics
- comfort and no exercise
- gives in to every plea
- result: a sick, sluggish dog

**The vet’s care**

- water, then plain food
- exercise and play
- company of other dogs
- result: a fit, lively dog
slides.narration: The central theme is the difference between pampering and real care. Mrs Pumphrey gives sweets, tonics and comfort, and gives in to every plea, and the result is a sick dog. The vet gives plain food, exercise and the company of other dogs, and the result is a healthy one. In answers, show this contrast clearly with evidence from both sides.

slides.heading: A web of themes

rows: Sweets and tonics make Tricki ill.
Plain food, exercise and company cure him; no medicine is used.
The vet acts firmly for his patient’s good.
The luggage, the gifts and the title.

visual.alt: Table of six themes with where each appears: pampering is not real care, common sense heals, professional responsibility, tact and kindness, humour and irony, and wealth without wisdom.

slides.narration: Around that central contrast sit other themes. Common sense heals, since no medicine is used. The vet shows professional responsibility and tact, acting firmly without humiliating the owner. Humour and irony run through the luggage, the gifts and the title. And the story quietly suggests that wealth can buy luxuries, but not good health or good judgement.

slides.heading: Check: the same mistake today
slides.narration: Check yourself. A grandmother gives her grandson sweets every time he cries, and he is often unwell. Whose approach from the story is she following?

slides.heading: Character: Mrs Pumphrey
slides.body_md: Every trait in an answer needs evidence, described in your own words.

rows: Cannot refuse Tricki’s begging for treats.
Thinks an overweight dog is underfed and adds tonics.
Is distraught when Tricki is taken away.
Sends eggs and wine to the surgery.
Thanks the vet warmly for a surgery that never happened.

visual.alt: Table of Mrs Pumphrey’s traits with evidence: loving but indulgent, ill-informed, emotional, generous, and grateful but unaware of the real cure.

slides.narration: Let us sketch Mrs Pumphrey. She is loving but indulgent, unable to refuse her pet anything. She is ill-informed, believing an overweight dog is underfed. She is emotional and generous, grieving when he leaves and sending gifts. And at the end she is grateful, but still unaware of what really cured him. She is foolish, but never cruel.

slides.heading: Character: the vet

rows: Sees the danger the moment he meets Tricki.
Advises gently; never blames Mrs Pumphrey.
Takes the dog away when advice fails.
Cures him with diet, exercise and company.
Owns up to enjoying the gifts.

visual.alt: Table of the vet’s traits with evidence: observant, tactful, firm, knowledgeable, and honest and humorous.

slides.narration: The vet is observant, spotting the danger at once. He is tactful, advising gently rather than blaming. He is firm when advice fails, taking the dog away. He is knowledgeable, curing Tricki without medicine. And he is honest and humorous, admitting that he enjoyed the gifts meant for his patient. These qualities make him a likeable and trustworthy narrator.

slides.heading: Comparing Mrs Pumphrey and the narrator
columns:
**Mrs Pumphrey**

- love led by feeling
- indulgence and luxury
- misreads the cure

**The narrator**

- love led by knowledge
- discipline and routine
- understands the cure, and smiles
slides.narration: Your syllabus asks you to compare these two characters. Mrs Pumphrey’s love is led by feeling; the vet’s is led by knowledge. She offers luxury; he offers routine and discipline. She misreads the cure as surgery; he knows the truth and quietly smiles. A strong answer gives evidence for each side and ends with a judgement about whose love is wiser.

slides.heading: Check: why the advice failed
slides.narration: Try this assertion and reason item. Decide whether each statement is true, and then whether the reason really explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Humour and irony
bullets: **Comic exaggeration:** a small dog leaves home with a bed, toys and coats.
**Gentle self-mockery:** the vets enjoy the gifts meant for the patient.
**Irony of the title:** a surgery that never happened.
**First-person narration:** a sensible observer we trust and enjoy.
**Light tone, serious point:** indulgence harms; common sense heals.
slides.narration: How does Herriot write? He uses comic exaggeration, such as Tricki’s luggage. He uses gentle self-mockery when the vets enjoy the gifts. The title carries irony, because the triumph of surgery involved no surgery. The first-person narrator is sensible and amusing. Behind the light tone lies a serious point about the harm that indulgence can do.

slides.heading: Irony and humour: SOYL’s own examples
slides.body_md: Practise spotting these techniques. These sentences are SOYL’s own, not from the story:
bullets: *The tortoise won the race, and the hare thanked his fast legs for teaching him patience.* — irony of outcome
*Grandma packed three sweaters, two blankets and a hot-water bottle for my one-night school trip in May.* — comic exaggeration of care
*The fitness coach praised the new protein shake, though the player had simply started sleeping eight hours.* — praise given to the wrong cause
slides.narration: Here are three sentences of our own. A hare thanks his fast legs after losing: irony of outcome. A grandmother packs blankets for a summer trip of one night: comic exaggeration of care. A coach praises a shake when sleep did the work: praise given to the wrong cause, just like Mrs Pumphrey. Now find Herriot’s own moments of irony in your textbook.

rows: to spoil with too much comfort
poor health from too little or the wrong food
a medicine or drink meant to strengthen
an operation; also a doctor’s or vet’s place of work
a gap between what seems and what is

visual.alt: Table of word meanings: indulgent, pamper, lethargic, malnutrition, tonic, convalescence, surgery with its two meanings, and irony.
visual.caption: Key words for this story with their meanings.

slides.narration: These words will help you write about the story. Indulgent means giving in to every wish, and to pamper is to spoil with comfort. Lethargic means sluggish. Malnutrition is poor health from bad or too little food. A tonic is meant to strengthen. Convalescence is the time of getting well. A surgery is an operation, and also a vet’s place of work.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a 6-mark answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* *Too much love can harm.* Discuss with reference to Tricki.
bullets: **Stand:** agree; love without wisdom harmed Tricki.
**Points + evidence:** sweets and tonics; no exercise; advice ignored because she could not refuse him.
**Turn:** the cure came from separation, routine and company.
**Value + conclusion:** real love sets limits, for pets and for children alike.

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a six mark answer. Take a stand: agree. Give points with evidence: the sweets and tonics, the lack of exercise, and the ignored advice. Then show the turn, when routine and company cured him. Finish by linking to a value, that real love sets limits, and apply it beyond the story, perhaps to children. Stay within the word limit.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Mrs Pumphrey overfed her Pekinese, Tricki, believing he was underfed.
The vet’s advice failed; Tricki fell ill and was taken to the surgery.
Water, plain food, exercise and other dogs cured him; the vets enjoyed her gifts.
She called the cure a triumph of surgery: the title is ironic.
Read the story in *Footprints without Feet*; write about it in your own words.

visual.alt: Flow of the story in six stages: a shock in the street; advice ignored; Tricki falls ill; off to the surgery; recovery among other dogs; and the ironic triumph of surgery.
visual.caption: The story in six stages (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Mrs Pumphrey overfed Tricki, thinking he was underfed. The vet’s advice failed, Tricki fell ill, and he was taken to the surgery. There, a plain routine and the company of other dogs cured him, while the vets enjoyed her gifts. She praised a triumph of surgery that never happened. Read the story in your textbook and write in your own words.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: 3-mark answers (40–50 words): point + evidence + explanation.
6-mark answers (100–120 words): stand → 3 points with evidence → value or theme → conclusion.
Facts often confused: Tricki had no operation; the tonics were Mrs Pumphrey’s idea, not the vet’s.
For comparison questions, give evidence for both Mrs Pumphrey and the vet.
Value questions: link the story to responsible care of pets or children.
slides.narration: Exam tips. In three mark answers, give a point, evidence and a short explanation. In six mark answers, take a stand and support it with three points, then link to a value. Get the facts right: Tricki had no operation, and the tonics were Mrs Pumphrey’s own idea. In comparisons, cover both characters. And in value questions, connect the story to real life.

sections.heading: 1. About the text and the author
sections.body_md:
**Read the story itself in your textbook, *Footprints without Feet* (NCERT supplementary reader).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the text.

**James Herriot** was the pen name of James Alfred Wight (1916–1995), a British vet who wrote humorous memoirs about his life as a country vet in Yorkshire. This story is told in the first person by the vet, with gentle humour and affection for both animals and their owners.

key_terms.definition_md: A true account of events from the writer’s own life.

sections.heading: 2. Summary (in SOYL’s words)
sections.body_md:
**The shock.** The vet meets Mrs Pumphrey and her Pekinese, Tricki, in the street and is alarmed at how fat and unwell the dog looks. Believing he is underfed, she has been adding malt, cod-liver oil and Horlicks to a diet of cakes and sweets. He advises less food and more exercise.

**Advice ignored.** She cannot refuse Tricki anything, so the treats continue, and he falls seriously ill.

**The surgery.** The vet takes Tricki to his surgery to control his diet and exercise. A distressed Mrs Pumphrey sends his bed, toys and coats with him.

**Recovery.** Tricki gets only water at first; then he grows interested in the other dogs, plays with them and eats eagerly. Mrs Pumphrey phones often and sends eggs and wine, which the vets enjoy.

**The ending.** Fit again, Tricki dashes to his owner when she comes to collect him. She calls the cure a triumph of surgery, though no operation took place.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Pampering is not real care:** indulgence makes Tricki ill.
- **Common sense heals:** plain food, exercise and company cure him without medicine.
- **Professional responsibility:** the vet acts firmly for his patient.
- **Tact and kindness:** he never humiliates the owner.
- **Humour and irony:** the luggage, the gifts and the title.
- **Wealth without wisdom:** money buys luxury, not health.

**Message:** real love for a pet (or a child) means meeting its true needs and setting limits, not giving in to every wish.

key_terms.definition_md: Allowing someone everything they want, even when it is bad for them.

sections.heading: 8. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**How this reader is examined:** the board sets 3-mark short answers (40–50 words; two of three) and a 6-mark long answer (100–120 words) on *Footprints without Feet*. It does not print extracts from this reader; SOYL’s commentary items are comprehension practice only.

**Short answers (3 marks):** point + evidence + explanation.

**Long answers (6 marks):** a clear stand; three points with evidence in your own words; a link to a value or theme; a one-line conclusion. Extrapolation tasks (Mrs Pumphrey’s diary, the vet’s letter, Tricki’s own account) must stay consistent with the story.

Re-read the story in *Footprints without Feet* before a test.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** Footprints short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words, two of three) and one long answer (6 marks, 100–120 words) (CBSE 2026-27, Section C). No extracts from this reader.

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant events, accurately used), interpretation (a clear, supported view or value), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Saying the vet operated on Tricki: there was no operation.
2. Saying the vet prescribed the tonics: they were Mrs Pumphrey’s idea.
3. Calling Mrs Pumphrey cruel: she is loving but foolish.
4. Forgetting the role of the other dogs in Tricki’s recovery.
5. Quoting lines from memory instead of explaining in your own words.

**Remember:** read the story in your textbook, *Footprints without Feet*.

questions.solution_md: Parts (a)–(c) recall the opening; (d) and (e) interpret it.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) a Pekinese

**(b)** malnutrition

**(c)** (d) to cut down Tricki’s food and give him more exercise

questions.passage_md: Herriot's story opens with a chance meeting. The vet sees Mrs Pumphrey out walking her Pekinese, Tricki, and is alarmed by what he sees: the dog has grown enormously fat, moves with effort and looks thoroughly unwell. Mrs Pumphrey has noticed only that her pet seems tired. Believing he is underfed, she has been adding malt, cod-liver oil and Horlicks to a diet already crowded with cakes and chocolates. The vet gently suggests less food and more exercise. She agrees in principle, yet the reader senses at once that a lady who cannot refuse her dog anything will not keep to such a plan for long.

children.stem_md: What kind of dog is Tricki in *A Triumph of Surgery*?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a Pekinese. Tricki is Mrs Pumphrey’s pet Pekinese.

children.stem_md: Mrs Pumphrey believed Tricki was suffering from ___, so she gave him extra tonics.
children.solution_md: She mistook his weakness for **malnutrition**.

Tricki’s departure, with his bed, toys and coats, is comic exaggeration that exposes how absurdly he is pampered. The gifts of eggs and wine, enjoyed by the vets instead of the patient, add light comedy and make the narrator human. The ending is the sharpest irony: Mrs Pumphrey praises a triumph of surgery when no operation took place. Behind the laughter lies the message that a simple, active life heals better than luxury, and that loving owners must listen to sense. Because readers are amused rather than lectured, they accept the lesson more easily.

questions.stem_md: What values does *A Triumph of Surgery* teach about responsibility towards animals in our care? Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Three or four values (balanced diet, exercise, company, expert advice, firmness, honesty) each linked to the story + conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md: The story teaches that responsibility towards animals means caring for their real needs. First, owners must give a balanced diet: Tricki’s sweets and tonics turned love into harm. Second, animals need exercise and the company of their own kind; Tricki recovered only when he ran and played with other dogs. Third, owners should respect expert advice, as Mrs Pumphrey failed to do until her pet became ill. The vet also shows the value of professional honesty and firmness, putting the patient’s welfare above an owner’s feelings. Finally, the story suggests that affection must be guided by knowledge. A responsible owner loves wisely, setting limits for the animal’s sake, not for personal satisfaction.

questions.stem_md: *A Triumph of Surgery* in *Footprints without Feet* was written by…
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** James Herriot. James Herriot, a vet and writer, is the author.

questions.stem_md: What was James Herriot’s profession, which gives *A Triumph of Surgery* its setting?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a veterinary surgeon. He was a working vet in Yorkshire.

questions.stem_md: Which of these did Mrs Pumphrey add to Tricki’s diet as a tonic?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** cod-liver oil. Malt, cod-liver oil and Horlicks were her extras.

questions.stem_md: Why did Mrs Pumphrey give Tricki extra tonics?

options.text_md: She thought he was underfed and weak.
She wanted him to grow bigger for a show.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** She thought he was underfed and weak. She mistook his sluggishness for malnutrition.

questions.stem_md: What was the real cause of Tricki’s illness?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** overfeeding and lack of exercise. Rich food and inactivity made him ill.

questions.stem_md: What step did the vet take when his advice to Mrs Pumphrey failed?

options.text_md: He operated on Tricki at once.
He reported Mrs Pumphrey to the police.
He took Tricki to his surgery to treat him there.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He took Tricki to his surgery to treat him there. He moved Tricki to the surgery to control his diet and exercise.

questions.stem_md: How did Tricki spend his first days at the vet’s surgery?

options.text_md: lying quietly, with only water to drink

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** lying quietly, with only water to drink. He was given only water and lay still at first.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best explains how Tricki was cured?

options.text_md: A difficult operation removed the problem.
A long rest in a soft bed healed him.
Plain food, exercise and the company of other dogs restored him.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Plain food, exercise and the company of other dogs restored him. An ordinary dog’s routine cured him, not surgery or medicine.

questions.stem_md: What did the narrator and his colleagues do with Mrs Pumphrey’s gifts for Tricki?

options.text_md: They sent them back to her.
They enjoyed the eggs and wine themselves.
They fed them all to Tricki.
They gave them to a charity.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They enjoyed the eggs and wine themselves. The vets enjoyed the gifts; the narrator admits it with humour.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of words best describes Mrs Pumphrey in *A Triumph of Surgery*?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** loving and indulgent. She loves Tricki but spoils him.

questions.stem_md: What is the overall tone of *A Triumph of Surgery*?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** light-hearted and gently ironic. Herriot tells the story with warm humour and irony.

questions.stem_md: Which message does Tricki’s story most strongly convey?

options.text_md: Rich food is the secret of good health.
Pets should never leave their owners.
Real care meets an animal’s needs instead of spoiling it.
Surgery is the answer to most illnesses.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Real care meets an animal’s needs instead of spoiling it. Indulgence harmed Tricki; sensible care cured him.

questions.stem_md: A grandmother gives her grandson sweets whenever he cries, and he is often unwell. Whose approach in *A Triumph of Surgery* does she follow?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Mrs Pumphrey’s. Like Mrs Pumphrey, she indulges instead of setting healthy limits.

questions.stem_md: From whose point of view is *A Triumph of Surgery* told?

options.text_md: the vet’s, in the first person

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the vet’s, in the first person. The vet narrates the events himself.

questions.stem_md: In *A Triumph of Surgery*, Mrs Pumphrey’s pet Tricki is a ___ dog.
questions.solution_md: Tricki is a **Pekinese**.

questions.stem_md: Tricki’s wealthy owner is Mrs ___.
questions.solution_md: His owner is Mrs **Pumphrey**.

questions.stem_md: At the surgery Tricki recovered through plain food, ___ and the ___ of other dogs.
questions.solution_md: His cure: plain food, **exercise** and the **company** of other dogs.

questions.stem_md: The title of Herriot’s story about Tricki is ___ because no operation was performed.
questions.solution_md: The title is **ironic**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Mrs Pumphrey gave Tricki malt and cod-liver oil.

**Reason (R):** The vet had prescribed these tonics to strengthen Tricki.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the tonics were Mrs Pumphrey’s own idea, because she thought he was underfed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Tricki’s cure in Herriot’s story was a triumph of surgery.

**Reason (R):** Tricki recovered through diet, exercise and the company of other dogs.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: there was no operation. R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The vet in *A Triumph of Surgery* enjoyed the eggs Mrs Pumphrey sent.

**Reason (R):** Mrs Pumphrey sent Tricki to the surgery with his bed and toys.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but sending his bed and toys does not explain why the vets enjoyed the eggs.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The vet’s first advice to Mrs Pumphrey did not improve Tricki’s health.

**Reason (R):** Mrs Pumphrey could not refuse Tricki’s pleading for treats.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: her indulgence undid the advice.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the vet in *A Triumph of Surgery* performed an operation on Tricki.
questions.solution_md: **False.** No operation was performed; diet and exercise cured him.

questions.stem_md: True or false: at the surgery Tricki was kept apart from all other dogs.
questions.solution_md: **False.** He lived and played with the other dogs, which helped him recover.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Mrs Pumphrey often telephoned the surgery for news of Tricki.
questions.solution_md: **True.** She called frequently, anxious about her pet.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Tricki returned to Mrs Pumphrey slimmer and livelier than before.
questions.solution_md: **True.** He came home fit and full of energy.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of *A Triumph of Surgery* in the order in which they happen.

options.text_md: Mrs Pumphrey collects a healthy Tricki.
The vet advises less food and more exercise.
Tricki starts playing with the other dogs.
The vet meets Mrs Pumphrey and an overweight Tricki in the street.
The vet takes Tricki to his surgery.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (c) → (b) → (f) → (d) → (a). Street meeting → advice → illness → the surgery → recovery with other dogs → reunion.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the stages of Tricki’s recovery at the vet’s surgery.

options.text_md: Tricki follows the other dogs about.
Tricki lies still, with only water to drink.
Tricki eats eagerly with the others at mealtimes.
Tricki races and plays with the other dogs.
Tricki begins to take an interest in his surroundings.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). Stillness → interest → following → play → eager eating.
